Kansas produces sturdy stems topped with intensely saturated, rounded double blooms in a clear cherry-red that holds its color well and resists fading in the sun. common_name: Monsieur Jules Elie Peony (Fragrant Silvery-Pink Double Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil, or set out potted plants in spring.

directions: Set bare-root divisions in early fall so the pink growth eyes sit just an inch or two beneath the soil surface, in a full-sun bed with fertile, well-drained soil. Stake plants or use a peony ring, since the huge domed flowers can become top-heavy after rain. Introduced in France in 1888, Monsieur Jules Elie remains one of the most widely grown heirloom peonies for its early, extremely fragrant, silvery-pink bomb-form blooms that fade to a paler blush as they age. Its sturdy foliage and reliable performance have kept it a garden and cut-flower favorite for well over a century.

directions: Plant divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun and well-drained, fertile soil, and avoid mulching too heavily over the crown since burial deeper than two inches inhibits flowering. Provide grow-through support early in spring growth to keep the heavy blooms upright through summer storms. Dating to 1881, Felix Crousse is a long-established French heirloom prized for its intensely fragrant, ruby-red double flowers with a faint silvery sheen on the outer petals. Its midseason bloom time and dependable vigor have made it a mainstay of cut-flower and cottage-garden peony collections for generations.

common_name: Miss America Peony (Gold Medal White Semi-Double Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil, or set out potted plants in spring.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and be patient the first year or two while the plant establishes its root system before flowering heavily. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage back to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover. Introduced in 1936 and awarded the American Peony Society's Gold Medal, Miss America bears huge, crepe-textured, semi-double white flowers with a subtle blush center and a boss of golden stamens. It remains one of the most celebrated early-blooming white peonies for both garden display and cutting.

common_name: Janice Brown Daylily (Compact Pink Reblooming Daylily)

planting.note: Divide and transplant bare-root fans in spring or late summer, spreading roots out in a shallow planting hole with the crown just below the soil surface.

directions: Plant bare-root fans in spring with the crown just below the soil surface, spacing them to allow the fountain-shaped foliage clumps room to expand. Grow in full sun with average, well-drained soil, and divide crowded clumps every three to four years to keep bloom production high. Janice Brown is a compact, early-to-rebloom daylily with soft pink, ruffled petals surrounding a distinct rose-pink eyezone and a green throat. Its dwarf habit and dependable rebloom cycle have made it a long-time favorite for borders and small-space gardens.

directions: Set bare-root fans in spring in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, fanning the roots downward and covering the crown with about an inch of soil. Water deeply after planting and keep beds weeded until clumps are established. Introduced in the early 1980s, Strutter's Ball produces velvety, deep purple-black blooms with a sharp, luminous green throat that provides striking contrast against the dark petals. Its rich color and vigorous clump-forming habit have kept it one of the most recognizable dark-toned daylilies in cultivation.

Blue Cadet forms a low, dense mound of small, rounded, blue-green leaves and produces abundant lavender flowers on short scapes in mid to late summer. Introduced by Paul Aden in the 1970s, it remains a popular compact edging and groundcover hosta for shaded borders.

This upright, vase-shaped cultivar bears large, ruffled, chartreuse-to-gold leaves that brighten as the season progresses, topped by pale lavender flowers in summer. Bred by Paul Aden, it is valued for its bold vertical form and vivid color in partly shaded borders.

directions: Space divisions closely in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to take advantage of Gold Edger's dense, mounding habit as an edging or groundcover plant. It tolerates more sun than many hostas, which helps deepen its golden leaf color. The small, rounded, chartreuse-gold leaves form a tidy low mound, with pale lavender flowers rising just above the foliage in summer. Introduced by Paul Aden, Gold Edger is a fast-multiplying, reliable cultivar long used for edging paths and shaded borders.
